title: All-hands: model safety framing + Q&A crib
content:
Purpose: personal crib for the CEO/lead moderation brief at the next all-hands. Keep short, empathetic, and operational. This is a scratchpad — unfinished phrasing and question fragments below.

Audience: whole company (~150). Primary goal: reassure product and eng teams that we acknowledge recent model-safety report, summarize immediate mitigations, and call out next steps + how teams can help. Secondary goal: set expectations externally (what we will say to customers).

High-level framing (30–45s):
- We found a safety regression in one of the model variants used for low-latency traffic. It was caught by our monitoring and some internal reports earlier this week.
- No customer data was exposed. The issue is model output quality aligned with safety guardrails — not auth/data leakage.
- We moved quickly: traffic was shifted to a safe fallback, we rolled a constrained model patch to dedicated pools, and we've opened an incident war room.

TL;DR for Qs:
- Impact: limited to a subset of requests in the hosted tier; small set of customers saw anomalous outputs.
- Customer postures: CS notified high-risk customers directly; account teams have scripts.
- Root cause (prelim): degradation triggered by a new tokenizer edge-case + negative interaction with recently added prompt templating heuristics.
- Fix status: mitigation in place; longer-term fix in code review and test harnesses being updated.

Suggested CEO lines (plain & short):
"We take safety seriously — when our systems behave unexpectedly we treat it like an incident. Teams acted fast, customers were prioritized, and we're working across ML, infra, and support to close the loop. I want to acknowledge the friction this causes and thank the people who jumped in."

Operational bullets (for the ops/eng audience):
- Immediate: traffic routing rule enacted to prefer model-v2-safe for all public hosted endpoints; cache invalidation triggered for prefix caching where anomaly detected.
- Monitoring: added a new anomaly detector for unusual sequence-level token distributions; increased sampling rate for flagged customers.
- CI/tests: adding targeted fuzz tests for tokenizer boundary cases; adding golden prompt set to the regression suite.
- Rollout: constrained patch will go to dedicated clusters tonight and private deploys will receive a recommended advisory.

Customer/comms scripts (for CS/AEs):
- Short statement to share: "We detected unexpected outputs in a small set of requests. Our automated systems flagged this, and we've routed traffic to a safer model variant while we complete a permanent fix. We're proactively reviewing any outputs for affected customers and will reach out if we find issues relevant to your data."
- If pressed for ETA: "Mitigation completed; root-cause fix is expected to land in the next 48–72 hours followed by staged validation."

Anticipated hard questions + short answers:
Q: Did any customer data leak?
A: No evidence of data exfiltration. We completed an audit of request logs and access patterns; results were negative. (Follow-up: security is performing a deeper review and will report to leadership if anything else shows up.)

Q: Why did this happen after our recent tokenizer improvements?
A: The tokenizer change handled some edge-cases better globally but created a low-frequency boundary condition that, combined with a specific prompt-engineering heuristic, produced outputs that failed our safety scoring heuristics. We're adding a targeted test and reverting the unsafe heuristic in the short term.

Q: Will this affect SLAs or credits?
A: Not at this time — we are tracking impact and will coordinate compensation through finance/CS if a customer impact threshold is met.

Q: How will you prevent regressions?
A: Three lines — increase fuzz testing and golden prompts in CI, expand anomaly detection on outputs (not just telemetry), and require a cross-functional sign-off for tokenizer or prompt-engineering changes.

Notes-to-self / presenter cues:
- Keep tone calm, accountable, solution-focused. Avoid technical deep-dives unless asked.
- Call out teams by function, not by individual names during all-hands (avoid blame).
- Ask for two things from the company: (1) patience for the next 48–72 hours while we validate fixes, (2) anyone with related concerns to flag via #safety-incident slack thread.

Follow-ups & action owners (quick list):
- ML (Rohit): push patch + regression tests (48–72 hrs).
- Infra (Kira): enforce routing + increase logging/sample rate (today).
- CS (Juno): customer triage and scripted outreach (immediate).
- Security: run deep audit of logs and provide report by EOD+2.

Unresolved / open questions (to chase in postmortem):
- Exact prompt templates that triggered the issue; need sample set and reproduction steps.
- Whether the tokenizer change should be partially reverted for older model variants.
- Any downstream partners (integrations) who may have cached outputs to invalidate.

Links & refs: (add live links before presenting)
- Incident doc: confluence:Model-Safety-Incident-2026-01-14 (placeholder)
- PR(s): github:repo/model-tokenizer-fix PR#56
- Slack thread: #safety-incident (pin important messages to incident doc)

Presentation plan (2–3 mins):
- 30s framing (what happened, non-technical).
- 45s what we did (mitigation + customer action).
- 45s what we are doing next + ask of org.
- Q&A (leave 5–6 mins).

Personal sticky notes (informal):
- Don’t promise exact ETA unless Rohit confirms.
- Avoid saying "no one affected" — say "limited subset" to avoid future contradictions.
- Remember to thank on-call and CS in open call.

-- end scratchpad --

(If I use this at the all-hands, I will trim the operational bullets to 3 lines and keep the Q&A to 3–4 expected questions. Save a copy to the incident doc before the meeting.)
